title.en: Geography: Human Geography of Tamil Nadu

text.en: Raju noticed the busy city of Chennai. "How do people live in different parts of Tamil Nadu?" he asked.

Human geography studies people and their activities. Tamil Nadu has a large population with high urbanisation, and Chennai, Coimbatore and Madurai are big cities. Literacy is high and the sex ratio is better than the national average.
Farming, fishing, industry and services are the main occupations. Transport includes a strong road and rail network, ports at Chennai, Ennore and Thoothukudi and airports at Chennai, Madurai and Coimbatore.
Tamil Nadu is known for its temples, handlooms, festivals and arts. Tourism, IT and education add to the economy, and we should preserve its heritage and the environment.

Tamil Nadu is known for its temples, handlooms, festivals and arts.
Tourism, IT and education add to the economy, and we should preserve its heritage and the environment.
Tamil Nadu stretches across India's southern tip, and its diverse terrain—from Western Ghats hills to Kaveri delta plains—shapes how 7.21 crore people live and work.
According to the 2011 Census, Tamil Nadu's population density is 555 persons per square kilometre—well above India's national average of 382.
Notice also the sex ratio: 996 females per 1,000 males in 2011, far better than the national average of 943, led by districts like The Nilgiris and Thanjavur.
Nearly 48.4 percent of Tamil Nadu lives in urban areas, making it India's most urbanised major state, anchored by Chennai, Coimbatore, Madurai, Tiruchirappalli and Salem.
Tamil Nadu's literacy rate reached 80.09 percent in 2011, with Kanniyakumari leading districts at over 91 percent thanks to public schools and midday meal schemes.
Agriculture remains the largest employer in rural areas, shaped by two monsoons—southwest and especially northeast—alongside river deltas and tank irrigation.
Paddy dominates the fertile Kaveri delta—called the Rice Bowl of Tamil Nadu—alongside millets like ragi and cumbu in drier tracts, plus sugarcane, cotton and groundnut.

board.text: Rice Bowl (Kaveri delta), millets & cash crops

text.en: On misty hill slopes of the Nilgiris, Anamalai and Kodaikanal, farmers grow tea, coffee, cardamom, pepper and temperate vegetables.

board.text: Plantation crops in Ghats & hill ranges

text.en: Across the 1,076-kilometre coastline from Chennai to Kanniyakumari, marine and inland fishing sustain coastal villages, centred at Nagapattinam, Thoothukudi and Rameswaram.
Tamil Nadu uses multipurpose river dams cleanly for irrigation, drinking water and hydroelectricity: Mettur on the Kaveri, Bhavanisagar, Vaigai and Papanasam.
Underground resources also power the state: Neyveli lignite fuels thermal electricity, Salem hosts iron ore and magnesite, and Cauvery delta holds natural gas.
Textile mills, sugar factories, cement works, leather tanneries and software parks employ millions of urban and semi-urban families.

board.text: Industries & IT corridor in major cities

text.en: Roadways knit even remote hamlets together: National Highways like NH-44 and state highways carry most passenger buses and farm freight.
Southern Railway serves Tamil Nadu with Broad Gauge corridors linking Chennai, Tiruchirappalli, Madurai and Coimbatore, plus Chennai Metro inside the capital.
Three major seaports—Chennai, Kamarajar Port at Ennore, and V.O. Chidambaranar Port at Thoothukudi—link factories and farms directly to global shipping lanes.
Airports at Chennai, Coimbatore, Madurai and Tiruchirappalli handle domestic and international passengers and high-value cargo.
Cultural and heritage tourism shines at Mahabalipuram, Thanjavur's Brihadeeswarar temple, Madurai Meenakshi temple, Rameswaram and Kanyakumari.
Hill stations like Ooty and Kodaikanal, plus Mudumalai and Gulf of Mannar biosphere reserves, attract eco-tourism while needing careful conservation.
Trade flows cleanly: Tamil Nadu exports textiles, leather footwear, vehicles, electronics and IT services while importing crude oil, coal and machinery.
Rapid growth brings pressure on cities and farms: groundwater depletion, urban solid waste, coastal erosion and heatwaves demand sustainable planning.
Rainwater harvesting, tank restoration (Kudimaramathu) and rooftop solar power help districts adapt to erratic monsoons.
Connect the whole state geographically: fertile deltas + 1,076 km coast + 80% literacy + dense ports & roads = balanced human development.
Understanding human geography helps citizens protect rivers, coasts and living heritage while sharing prosperity across every district.

problem.en: How do Tamil Nadu's physical features and literacy rate together explain its varied occupations and high urbanisation?

why.en: The fertile Kaveri and Vaigai deltas support intensive paddy cultivation, while dry interior plains favour millets, cotton and groundnut.

text.en: Connect coastline & minerals to trade & power.

why.en: A 1,076-km coastline supports fishing and major ports at Chennai, Ennore and Thoothukudi, while Neyveli lignite supplies electricity.

text.en: Connect 80.09% literacy to modern cities.

why.en: High school and college enrolment trains skilled workers for engineering, textiles, healthcare and IT across five major urban corridors.
